title: MS Word
summary: Word-processing features, formatting defaults, mail merge, references and the Word shortcut set. Shift analyses regularly put 2-4 CKT questions on Word - mostly shortcut keys and default settings.

subtopics.title: Word interface, views and basics
subtopics.concept:
MS Word (part of Microsoft Office since 1983) is a word processor used for documents such as letters and reports.

**Interface:** Ribbon tabs (File, Home, Insert, Design, Layout, References, Mailings, Review, View) hold grouped commands; the Quick Access Toolbar sits above it (customisable); the Status bar (bottom) shows page number, word count and zoom; the **File tab** opens Backstage view (New/Open/Save/Print/Options).

**Document views:** Print Layout (**default**), Read Mode, Web Layout, Outline, Draft. Zoom from 10% to 500%. **Word wrap** moves text to the next line automatically - pressing Enter starts a new paragraph, not a new line. **AutoCorrect** fixes typos as you type (teh -> the); AutoText/Quick Parts stores reusable blocks. The Office Clipboard keeps up to **24** cut/copied items; the Format Painter copies formatting (double-click to lock it). Templates (.dotx) give ready-made layouts; the normal template is Normal.dotm.

**Document window keys:** Ctrl+N new, Ctrl+O open, Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+P print, Ctrl+W close document, Alt+F4 exit Word.

tricks.title: Views ladder
tricks.body: Default view = **Print Layout** (what you print is what you see). Reading = book mode; Web = browser look; Outline = headings hierarchy; Draft = bare text. If a question says 'default', Print Layout is the answer.

example.q: Default document view in Word?
example.solution: Print Layout.

tricks.title: Backstage tab
tricks.body: New, Open, Save, Print, Options live under the **File** tab (Backstage view), not the Home ribbon. Any 'where do you find Print/Options' question -> File tab.

example.q: Which tab contains the Options dialog?
example.solution: File (Backstage view).

mistakes: Pressing Enter at each line end - word wrap handles line breaks; Enter creates paragraphs.
Calling the status bar's word-count the only count - Word Count is also a dialog (Ctrl+Shift+G, Review tab).
Assuming Draft is the default view.
subtopics.notes:
### What MS Word is
**MS Word** is a **word processor** — software used to create, edit, format and print text documents such as letters, reports, applications and resumes. It was first released in **1983** and has been part of the **Microsoft Office** suite since Office began. A file made in Word is called a **document**.

### The parts of the Word window
- **Title bar** — the top strip showing the file name and the program name.
- **Quick Access Toolbar (QAT)** — tiny buttons at the very top-left; by default it holds **Save, Undo and Redo**. You can add more buttons.
- **Ribbon** — the wide band of commands below the title bar. Commands sit in **groups** (like Clipboard, Font, Paragraph) inside **tabs**: **File, Home, Insert, Design, Layout, References, Mailings, Review, View**. The small arrow at the bottom-right corner of a group opens that group's full dialog box.
- **File tab (Backstage view)** — clicking File does not show a ribbon; it opens a full-screen menu called the **Backstage view**: New, Open, Save, Save As, Print, Share, Export, Close and **Options** (all settings live here). Document properties and printing are managed here.
- **Work area / page** — the white sheet where you type.
- **Status bar** — the bottom strip. It shows the **page number (Page x of y), the word count**, the proofing/language icon, the **view buttons** and the **zoom slider**. You can right-click it to choose what it shows.
- **Scroll bars and zoom** — Ctrl + mouse scroll zooms in and out; zoom changes only how large the page looks, never the print size.

### The five views of Word (View tab, also on the status bar)
| View | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Print Layout** | **Default view**; shows the page exactly as it will print |
| **Read Mode** | Full-screen reading; hides most editing tools |
| **Web Layout** | Shows how the text would look as a web page |
| **Outline** | Works with headings; good for restructuring long reports |
| **Draft** | Plain text view; hides pictures, headers and footers to save time |

### Everyday basics exams keep asking
- **Word wrap** — when a line is full, Word moves the next word to a new line by itself. You press **Enter only to end a paragraph**, not at the end of every line.
- **Undo (Ctrl+Z)** cancels your last action and **Redo (Ctrl+Y)** brings it back; both sit on the QAT.
- **Word count** — on the status bar, or Review tab, or Ctrl+Shift+G.
- **Navigation pane** (View tab, or Ctrl+F) finds words and jumps between headings.
- **Templates** — ready-made designs (resume, invoice, calendar) listed under File, New.
- **Help** — F1 opens Word's help.

### Quick revision
- Word = word processor, part of MS Office, first released 1983; document file.
- Ribbon tabs: File, Home, Insert, Design, Layout, References, Mailings, Review, View.
- File tab opens **Backstage view** (New, Open, Print, Options).
- QAT default buttons: Save, Undo (Ctrl+Z), Redo (Ctrl+Y).
- Status bar: page number, word count, zoom; **Print Layout is the default view**.
- Enter ends a paragraph — word wrap ends lines automatically.

patterns.name: Which tab holds this feature?
patterns.howToSpot: The stem names a Word feature (Track Changes, Word Art, Page Number, Mail Merge, Spelling) and asks the ribbon tab it lives on, or gives a tab and asks what it contains.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the tab map: Home = formatting, Insert = objects (table, picture, chart, header/footer, page number, text box, symbol), Design = themes, Layout = margins/orientation/size, References = TOC/footnotes, Mailings = mail merge, Review = spelling/track changes/word count, View = views/zoom/navigation.
2. File is not a ribbon tab — it opens Backstage (New, Open, Print, Options).
3. Traps: Track Changes is Review (not Insert); page numbers are Insert (not Layout); TOC is References (not Insert).

example.q: In MS Word, the Track Changes option is found on which tab?
example.solution: **Review** — the tab for checking and teamwork: spelling, thesaurus, comments, Track Changes and Compare.

patterns.name: View identification and purpose
patterns.howToSpot: The stem describes a need (see the page as printed, read without distraction, reorder pages, plain text without pictures) or names a view and asks its purpose or which one is the default.
patterns.logic:
1. Print Layout = default, shows the page as it prints. Read Mode = distraction-free reading. Web Layout = as a web page. Outline = headings only, restructure. Draft = plain text, hides images/headers.
2. 'See margins and page breaks while typing' means Print Layout.
3. Default-view questions: the answer is Print Layout, never Draft.

example.q: Which view of MS Word is the default view?
example.solution: **Print Layout** — it shows the page, margins and breaks exactly as the document will print.

patterns.name: Status bar, word count and zoom
patterns.howToSpot: The stem asks what the status bar shows, where the word count appears, or what zoom does to the print size.
patterns.logic:
1. Status bar (bottom) shows Page x of y, word count, language, view buttons and zoom slider.
2. Word count: status bar OR Review tab OR Ctrl+Shift+G.
3. Zoom (Ctrl+scroll or slider) changes only the on-screen size — printing size is fixed by font size.

example.q: In MS Word, the word count of a document can be seen on the —
example.solution: **Status bar and the Review tab** (also Ctrl+Shift+G). The status bar keeps a live count while you type.

patterns.name: Word basics and Backstage view
patterns.howToSpot: Direct recall: which program is a word processor, what a Word file is called, what the File tab offers, what the Quick Access Toolbar holds.
patterns.logic:
1. Word = word processor; its file = document; part of Microsoft Office suite.
2. File tab opens **Backstage view**: New, Open, Save/Save As, Print, Share, Export, Options.
3. QAT default = Save, Undo, Redo — customizable from its drop-down arrow.

example.q: Clicking the File tab in MS Word opens the —
example.solution: **Backstage view** — the full-screen menu for New, Open, Save As, Print, Share, Export and Options. The other tabs show ribbon commands instead.

patterns.name: Undo, Redo and word wrap
patterns.howToSpot: Questions on which keys cancel the last action, bring it back, or what Word does automatically when a line is full.
patterns.logic:
1. Undo = Ctrl+Z, Redo = Ctrl+Y (both also on the Quick Access Toolbar).
2. Word wrap: the next word moves to a new line automatically — pressing Enter at every line end creates broken paragraphs.
3. Enter ends a **paragraph**, Shift+Enter ends a line within the same paragraph.

example.q: When a typed line reaches the right margin, MS Word —
example.solution: **moves the next word to a new line automatically (word wrap)**. The Enter key is needed only to start a new paragraph.

subtopics.title: Formatting text, paragraphs and pages
subtopics.concept:
**Character formatting:** bold (Ctrl+B), italic (Ctrl+I), underline (Ctrl+U), font face/size, colour, highlight, Strikethrough, Subscript (Ctrl+=), Superscript (Ctrl+Shift+=), Change Case (Shift+F3: Sentence case -> lowercase -> UPPERCASE -> Capitalize Each Word -> tOGGLE cASE), Grow/Shrink font (Ctrl+Shift+> / < , or Ctrl+] / [ in 1-pt steps). Default font: Calibri 11 pt from Word 2007-2021; Office 365/2024 switched the default to **Aptos 12 pt** (2023).

**Paragraph formatting:** alignment - left (**default**), centre (Ctrl+E), right (Ctrl+R), justify (Ctrl+J); line spacing single/double (Ctrl+1/Ctrl+2)/1.5 (Ctrl+5); spacing before/after (Word 2013+ default 1.08 lines with 8 pt after); indentation (Ctrl+M in, Ctrl+Shift+M out; Ctrl+T hanging indent); bullets/numbering/multilevel lists; borders and shading; Drop Cap (Insert tab).

**Page setup (Layout tab):** margins, size (A4/Letter), orientation **portrait (default) / landscape**; columns (1 default); line numbers, hyphenation. Insert: **page break (Ctrl+Enter)**, section breaks (change layout mid-document), page numbers, header/footer (default header/footer position is 1.25 cm / 0.5 inch from edge), watermark, page colour, page border, cover page. Headers/footers repeat automatically on every page unless sections differ.

tricks.title: Alignment letters
tricks.body: The shortcut letter sits inside the word: c**t**rE? No - simply: **L**eft=Ctrl+**L**, C**E**nter=Ctrl+**E**, **R**ight=Ctrl+**R**, **J**ustify=Ctrl+**J**. Only Centre breaks the pattern with E.

example.q: Shortcut for justify alignment?
example.solution: Ctrl+J.

tricks.title: Spacing numbers
tricks.body: Line-spacing shortcuts ARE the spacing: Ctrl+**1** single, Ctrl+**2** double, Ctrl+**5** 1.5. (Five looks like S for single-and-a-half.)

example.q: Shortcut for 1.5 line spacing?
example.solution: Ctrl+5.

tricks.title: Case cycle
tricks.body: **Shift+F3** cycles case: start at 'hello world' -> HELLO WORLD -> Hello World. Press it repeatedly to see all five styles; no menu needed.

example.q: Shortcut to cycle through case styles?
example.solution: Shift+F3.

mistakes: Using Ctrl+H for hyperlink - Ctrl+H is Replace; hyperlink is **Ctrl+K**.
Thinking landscape is the default orientation - portrait is.
subtopics.notes:
### Three levels of formatting
Formatting means changing how text looks. Word formats at three levels: **character** (letters), **paragraph** (whole blocks) and **page** (the whole sheet).

### Character formatting (Home tab, Font group)
| Action | Shortcut |
|---|---|
| **Bold** | Ctrl+B |
| **Italic** | Ctrl+I |
| **Underline** | Ctrl+U |
| **Subscript** (H2O style) | Ctrl+= |
| **Superscript** (x2 style) | Ctrl+Shift+= |
| Grow / shrink font | Ctrl+Shift+> / Ctrl+< |
| Change case cycle | Shift+F3 |

**Shift+F3** cycles selected text through UPPERCASE, lowercase and Capitalise Each Word — a favourite exam shortcut. Other font tools: font face (type style), font size (measured in **points**), colour, **text highlight colour** (marker behind text), **Strikethrough**, and **Format Painter** (copies formatting from one place to another).

### Paragraph formatting (Home tab, Paragraph group)
| Alignment | Shortcut | Look |
|---|---|---|
| Left (default) | Ctrl+L | ragged right edge |
| Centre | Ctrl+E | symmetric |
| Right | Ctrl+R | ragged left edge |
| Justify | Ctrl+J | **both edges straight** |

**Justified** text is aligned on both the left and the right edge — used in newspapers and formal reports. Line spacing shortcuts: **Ctrl+1 = single, Ctrl+5 = 1.5 lines, Ctrl+2 = double**. Other paragraph tools: bullets and numbering (a numbered/ bulleted list starts automatically when a line begins with 1. or *), indentation, borders and shading. A hard **page break** is inserted with **Ctrl+Enter**.

### Page formatting (Layout tab)
- **Margins** — blank space around the text; default (Normal) margins are **1 inch on all four sides**.
- **Orientation** — **Portrait** (taller than wide) is the **default**; **Landscape** turns the page sideways for wide tables.
- **Paper size** — A4 is the common default in India; Legal and Letter are other sizes.
- **Columns** — splits text into newspaper-style columns.
- **Header** (text at the top of every page) and **Footer** (bottom of every page) come from the Insert tab; page numbers are inserted in the footer.

### Default look of a new document
A new document uses the **Calibri** font at **11 points** (Word 2007 to 2021; newer Microsoft 365 builds ship with Aptos 12), left alignment and single spacing. Theme colours and the default style set can be changed from the Design tab.

### Quick revision
- Ctrl+B/I/U bold-italic-underline; Ctrl+= subscript, Ctrl+Shift+= superscript.
- Shift+F3 changes case; Ctrl+L/E/R/J left-centre-right-justify.
- Ctrl+1 / Ctrl+5 / Ctrl+2 = single / 1.5 / double line spacing.
- Portrait is the default orientation; Normal margins = 1 inch.
- Default font Calibri 11 (Office 2007-2021); Ctrl+Enter = page break.
- Ctrl+H is Replace, **Ctrl+K is hyperlink** — the classic trap pair.

patterns.name: Character-formatting shortcuts
patterns.howToSpot: 'The shortcut of Bold/Italic/Underline/Subscript/Superscript', 'which key changes the case', or a matched pair where one shortcut is shifted to the wrong action.
patterns.logic:
1. Core trio: Bold Ctrl+B, Italic Ctrl+I, Underline Ctrl+U (B-I-U = the letters themselves).
2. Subscript Ctrl+= , Superscript Ctrl+Shift+= (superscript needs the extra Shift).
3. Case cycle = Shift+F3 (lower, UPPER, Capitalise Each Word). Grow/shrink = Ctrl+Shift+> / Ctrl+<.

example.q: The keyboard shortcut to apply superscript in MS Word is:
example.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+=** — the same key as subscript (Ctrl+=) with Shift added. Both are toggles: press again to return to normal text.

patterns.name: Alignment shortcut matching
patterns.howToSpot: The stem gives an alignment (left, right, centre, justify) and asks the shortcut, or shows Ctrl+E / Ctrl+J and asks what they do.
patterns.logic:
1. Ctrl+L left, Ctrl+R right, Ctrl+E centre, Ctrl+J justify — remember **J = Justify (both edges)**.
2. Default alignment of Word = left.
3. Justify is used in newspapers and formal documents; centre is used in titles and invitations.

example.q: Which shortcut justifies the selected paragraph in MS Word?
example.solution: **Ctrl+J** — straightens both the left and right edges. Ctrl+E centres, Ctrl+L/Ctrl+R align left/right.

patterns.name: Line spacing and paragraph keys
patterns.howToSpot: 'Single / 1.5 / double line spacing shortcut', 'which shortcut inserts a page break', bullets and numbering questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Ctrl+1 single, Ctrl+5 (five = one-and-a-half on the number row) 1.5, Ctrl+2 double.
2. Page break = Ctrl+Enter; a hard break starts the next text on a fresh page.
3. Bullets/numbering sit in the Home tab, Paragraph group.

example.q: In MS Word, double line spacing is applied by —
example.solution: **Ctrl+2** (Ctrl+1 = single, Ctrl+5 = 1.5 lines). All three are toggles for the selected paragraphs.

patterns.name: Page setup: margins, orientation, size
patterns.howToSpot: The stem asks the default orientation, the default margin width, where page size or columns are set, or a scenario needing landscape.
patterns.logic:
1. Default orientation = **Portrait**; Landscape = sideways, used for wide tables.
2. Default (Normal) margins = **1 inch** on all four sides.
3. Margins, Orientation, Size and Columns all live on the **Layout** tab (older name: Page Layout).

example.q: The default orientation of a page in MS Word is:
example.solution: **Portrait** — height greater than width. Landscape (width greater than height) must be chosen manually from the Layout tab.

patterns.name: Default font facts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Default font of MS Word 2007/2010/2016' or a pair-matching of Office version with its default font and size.
patterns.logic:
1. Word 2007 to 2021 default font = **Calibri 11 point** (before 2007 it was Times New Roman 12).
2. Newer Microsoft 365 builds ship with **Aptos 12** — beware version wording in the stem.
3. Font size is measured in **points** (72 points = 1 inch).

example.q: The default font of Word 2007 to Word 2019 documents is:
example.solution: **Calibri, 11 point** — replacing Times New Roman 12 of Word 97-2003. Newest Microsoft 365 versions have moved to Aptos 12.

subtopics.title: Mail merge, references, review and macros
subtopics.concept:
**Mail merge** creates many personalised documents from one template: (1) write the main document, (2) attach a data source (Excel list, Access table, Outlook contacts), (3) insert merge fields («Name»), (4) preview, (5) merge to letters, e-mails, envelopes or labels. Tabs: Mailings -> Start Mail Merge. Used for certificates, call letters, mailing labels.

**Tables:** Insert -> Table; a table is rows x columns of cells. Table formulas work like `=SUM(ABOVE)`, `=AVERAGE(LEFT)` (Layout tab -> Formula). Convert text to table and vice versa.

**References tab:** automatic **Table of Contents** (needs Heading 1-3 **styles** applied first), footnotes (**Alt+Ctrl+F** - note at page bottom) vs endnotes (**Alt+Ctrl+D** - at document end), citations/bibliography, captions, index.

**Review tab:** Spelling & Grammar (**F7**), Thesaurus (**Shift+F7**), Word Count (**Ctrl+Shift+G**; words/characters/paragraphs/lines), **Track Changes** (edits recorded for review), Comments (Ctrl+Alt+M), Compare, Restrict Editing, Protect Document (password to open/modify; Mark as Final).

**Macros:** recorded/written sequences of commands (VBA); run with **Alt+F8**; files with macros saved as **.docm**; macro security warns about macro viruses.

tricks.title: No style, no TOC
tricks.body: An automatic Table of Contents is built from **Heading styles**. If the headings were bolded by hand (not styled), the TOC comes out empty - the classic trap.

example.q: Auto TOC requires?
example.solution: Headings formatted with built-in Heading styles.

tricks.title: Footnote = F below, Endnote = D for 'enD'

example.q: Shortcut to insert a footnote?
example.solution: Alt+Ctrl+F.

tricks.title: Merge field marks
tricks.body: Mail-merge placeholders appear inside guillemets - «Name». Data comes from the **data source**; the letter layout lives in the **main document**. Two parts, always.

example.q: In mail merge, the Excel list of recipients is the?
example.solution: Data source.

mistakes: Believing Track Changes is on the Insert tab - it is on Review.
Trying to build an automatic TOC from manually bolded text - styles are compulsory.
Calling Ctrl+Shift+G the Thesaurus - that opens Word Count; Shift+F7 is Thesaurus.
subtopics.notes:
### Mail merge — one letter, many receivers
**Mail merge** creates many personalised copies of one document — each receiver sees their own name and address, but the body text is typed only once. It lives on the **Mailings** tab and has **three components**:

1. **Main document** — the letter (or envelope, label, e-mail) with fixed text and empty slots.
2. **Data source** — the list of receivers: an Excel sheet, an Access table or Outlook contacts, with one column per detail (Name, City, PIN...).
3. **Merged document** — the final output: one finished copy per record.

**Steps:** write the main document, connect the data source (Start Mail Merge, Select Recipients), place **merge fields** (Insert Merge Field — the slot shows as <<Name>>) where each detail should appear, **Preview Results**, then **Finish & Merge** (print, or create a new document, or send e-mails). Classic exam uses: admission letters, result letters, address labels, envelopes, certificates and ID cards.

### References tab — TOC, footnotes and citations
- **Table of Contents (TOC)** — an automatic chapter list with page numbers. It can only be built from **heading styles** (Heading 1, Heading 2...): apply the styles first, then References, Table of Contents. After editing, right-click and **Update Field** (or press **F9**) to refresh page numbers.
- **Footnote** — a small note at the **bottom of the page**; insert with References, Insert Footnote or **Ctrl+Alt+F**.
- **Endnote** — a note collected at the **end of the document (or section)**; **Ctrl+Alt+D**.
- **Citations and bibliography** — References tab tools that record sources of quotes and generate the reference list automatically.

### Review tab — checking and teamwork
| Tool | Shortcut | Work |
|---|---|---|
| Spelling & Grammar | **F7** | checks mistakes |
| Thesaurus | **Shift+F7** | suggests synonyms |
| Word Count dialog | Ctrl+Shift+G | counts pages, words, characters |
| Track Changes | Ctrl+Shift+E | marks every edit for reviewers |
| New Comment | Ctrl+Alt+M | sticky note on selected text |

Track Changes and Comments are how two people edit one file without losing anyone's work. **Compare** shows differences between two versions of a document.

### Macros — record and replay
A **macro** is a **recorded series of commands** that Word replays with one click or shortcut — useful for repeated jobs (a fixed header block, a standard table). You record it (View tab or Developer tab, Record Macro), and Word saves the steps. Macro-enabled documents use the **.docm** extension, and **macro viruses** spread through such files, which is why Word warns before enabling macros.

### Quick revision
- Mail merge = main document + data source + merged output (Mailings tab).
- Merge field placeholder looks like <<Name>>.
- TOC needs **heading styles**; update with F9.
- Footnote = bottom of page (Ctrl+Alt+F); Endnote = end of document (Ctrl+Alt+D).
- F7 spelling, Shift+F7 thesaurus, Ctrl+Shift+E Track Changes, Ctrl+Alt+M comment.
- Macro = recorded command series; macro files are .docm.

patterns.name: Mail-merge components and steps
patterns.howToSpot: The stem names the three components, orders the steps, or gives a scenario (result letters to 500 students) and asks the feature or the tab used.
patterns.logic:
1. Components: **main document + data source + merged document**.
2. Steps: write main letter, attach data source, insert merge fields (<<Name>>), preview, finish & merge.
3. Data source = Excel sheet / Access table / Outlook contacts; everything happens on the **Mailings** tab.

example.q: To send the same offer letter to 300 applicants with each name filled in, the Word feature used is:
example.solution: **Mail merge** (Mailings tab) — one main document plus a data source list; Word generates 300 personalised copies in one run.

patterns.name: Footnote vs endnote vs TOC
patterns.howToSpot: The stem contrasts footnotes and endnotes, asks their shortcuts, or asks what an automatic Table of Contents is built from.
patterns.logic:
1. Footnote = bottom of the **page** (Ctrl+Alt+F); Endnote = **end of document/section** (Ctrl+Alt+D).
2. TOC is built only from **heading styles**, not from manually bolded lines; refresh with F9.
3. All three tools sit on the **References** tab.

example.q: In MS Word, a note printed at the bottom of the same page is called a:
example.solution: **Footnote** (inserted with Ctrl+Alt+F or References, Insert Footnote). The same note collected at the end of the document would be an endnote (Ctrl+Alt+D).

patterns.name: Review-tab tools and shortcuts
patterns.howToSpot: Shortcut recall — spelling, thesaurus, word count, comment — or a statement question about Track Changes and Comments.
patterns.logic:
1. Spelling & Grammar = **F7**; Thesaurus = **Shift+F7**; Word Count dialog = Ctrl+Shift+G; New Comment = Ctrl+Alt+M; Track Changes = Ctrl+Shift+E.
2. Track Changes **records every edit** so co-authors can accept or reject it; it is on the Review tab.
3. Classic trap: Ctrl+Shift+G opens Word Count, not the thesaurus.

example.q: In MS Word, the Thesaurus opens with which key?
example.solution: **Shift+F7** — it suggests synonyms for the selected word. F7 (without Shift) runs the spelling and grammar check.

patterns.name: Macro purpose and macro files
patterns.howToSpot: 'A macro is', 'which file stores macros', or a scenario of a repeated task being automated with one click.
patterns.logic:
1. Macro = a **recorded series of commands** replayed by one click or shortcut key.
2. Macro-enabled files carry **m**: .docm (document), .dotm (template).
3. Macro viruses travel inside macro files — Word asks before enabling them.

example.q: A macro in MS Word is best described as:
example.solution: **A recorded series of commands that can be replayed with a single click or key** — used to automate repeated steps. Macro files use the .docm extension.

subtopics.title: File types and defaults
subtopics.concept:
| Extension | Meaning |
|---|---|
| .docx | Word document, Word 2007+ (Office Open XML; the X = XML) |
| .doc | Word 97-2003 document (still opens in new Word) |
| .dotx / .dotm / .docm | Template / macro-enabled template / macro-enabled document |
| .rtf | Rich Text Format (portable formatting) |
| .odt | OpenDocument text (LibreOffice) |
| .pdf | Portable Document Format (Word can Save As/Export to PDF) |

**Defaults to memorise:** new file name **Document1**; default font Calibri 11 pt (2007-2021) / Aptos 12 pt (Office 365, 2023 onwards); default alignment left; default line spacing 1.08 (Word 2013+) with 8 pt space-after; default view Print Layout; default orientation portrait; default A4 (or Letter in US installs); normal template **Normal.dotm**; default author name from Office account settings.

tricks.title: X = XML = 2007+
tricks.body: Across Office: **docx/xlsx/pptx = 2007 and later** (Office Open XML, zip-compressed); the 3-letter .doc/.xls/.ppt = 97-2003. If a question mentions the X, it means XML.

example.q: Default extension of Word 2019 documents?
example.solution: .docx.

tricks.title: Font eras
tricks.body: Word 2003 default = Times New Roman 12. Word 2007-2021 = **Calibri 11**. Office 365 (mid-2023) & Office 2024 = **Aptos 12**. Exams still ask Calibri 11 most often.

example.q: Default font of Word 2016?
example.solution: Calibri, 11 pt.

mistakes: Answering .doc for a Word 2007+ default - .doc is the 97-2003 format.
Saying Calibri 12 or Aptos 11 - pairings are Calibri 11 and Aptos 12.
Thinking .docx files cannot be opened in Word 2003 - compatibility packs/converters exist.
subtopics.notes:
### Why file extensions matter
Every Word file ends with a **dot + letters** called the **extension**. It tells Windows which program should open the file and which format the data is stored in. Exams test whether you know the default modern format, the old format and the special formats.

### The Word extension family
| Extension | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **.docx** | **Default** Word document from **Word 2007 onwards**; Office Open XML format — the **X stands for XML** |
| **.doc** | Word **97-2003** format (older files still open in new Word) |
| **.docm** | Macro-enabled document (m = macro) |
| **.dotx** | Template — a ready pattern for new documents |
| **.dotm** | Macro-enabled template |
| **.pdf** | Fixed print-ready file; Word can **export or Save As** PDF |
| **.rtf** | Rich Text Format — keeps simple formatting, opens in many editors |
| **.odt** | OpenDocument Text — the format of free office suites |
| **.txt** | Plain text only — no formatting at all |

### The X = XML rule
From Office **2007**, every Office program switched to **Office Open XML** formats, and the new extensions gained an **X**: Word .doc**x**, Excel .xls**x**, PowerPoint .ppt**x**. If the exam shows an option with an X and an identical option without, the X one is the modern default and the plain one is the 97-2003 file. A fourth letter **m** (dotm, xlsm, pptm) always means **macro-enabled**. This one rule answers a whole family of questions across Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

### Facts asked about formats
- A **.docx** file cannot be opened by Word 2003 **natively**, but Microsoft released a **Compatibility Pack** that lets the old Word open the new format.
- **Save As** (F12) is where you pick a different format; the default can be changed in File, Options, Save.
- **PDF** is the format chosen when a document must look identical on every computer and printer — ideal for forms and e-books.
- **.rtf** and **.odt** are cross-program formats: they open outside Microsoft Office too.
- Templates (.dotx) open as an **untitled new copy**, protecting the original design.
- **.txt** loses all bold, italic, fonts and pictures — only characters survive.

### Quick revision
- Default: **.docx** (Word 2007+, X = XML); legacy: .doc (97-2003).
- m = macro: .docm document, .dotm template; .dotx = template.
- Export/Save As **.pdf** for fixed printing; .rtf and .odt are cross-software; .txt = no formatting.
- The X rule: docx/xlsx/pptx are all 2007+ Office Open XML formats.
- Word 2003 opens .docx only with the Compatibility Pack.
- Templates open as a fresh untitled copy.

patterns.name: Default extension of a Word file
patterns.howToSpot: 'The default extension of MS Word 2007/2010/2016 is' — four extensions, one right. Sometimes reversed: an extension is given, the program is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Modern default = **.docx** (Word 2007 onwards); the X means Office Open XML.
2. .doc = Word 97-2003 legacy file.
3. For Excel the pair is .xlsx/.xls and for PowerPoint .pptx/.ppt — the X rule works across all three programs.

example.q: The default file extension of a Word 2016 document is:
example.solution: **.docx** — Office Open XML format, standard since Word 2007. .doc belongs to Word 97-2003.

patterns.name: doc vs docx legacy trap
patterns.howToSpot: A pair like .doc/.docx (or all four Office pairs) with the question 'which is the older format' or 'which will a Word 2003 file carry'.
patterns.logic:
1. 97-2003 = .doc; 2007+ = .docx. Older Word could not open .docx without the **Compatibility Pack**.
2. In mixed-option questions, the X-less option is always the older format.
3. .docx files are also smaller and recover data better (XML parts) than .doc.

example.q: Which file format was used by Word 97-2003?
example.solution: **.doc** — the binary format before Office Open XML (.docx) arrived with Word 2007.

patterns.name: Template and macro extensions
patterns.howToSpot: The stem asks the extension of a template or a macro-enabled file, or shows .dotx/.docm and asks what it is.
patterns.logic:
1. Template = .dotx; macro-enabled document = .docm; macro-enabled template = .dotm.
2. m always = macro; t = template.
3. Opening a template creates a fresh untitled copy, so the design stays safe.

example.q: A Word file saved with macros enabled carries which extension?
example.solution: **.docm** — m = macro. A macro-enabled template is .dotm and a plain template is .dotx.

patterns.name: Export and cross-software formats
patterns.howToSpot: 'To share a document that prints identically everywhere, save as —' or identification of .rtf / .odt / .txt / .pdf meanings.
patterns.logic:
1. **PDF** = fixed layout, prints identically on any machine — the sharing choice.
2. .rtf = Rich Text Format (basic formatting, opens in many editors); .odt = OpenDocument (free office suites); .txt = plain characters only, no formatting.
3. Save As (F12) is where the format is changed.

example.q: Ravi wants his resume to look exactly the same on any computer or printer. He should save it as —
example.solution: **PDF** — a fixed-layout format that keeps fonts and layout frozen. Word exports or Save-As to PDF from the File menu.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem names a Word action (bold, case change, footnote, thesaurus, page break) and asks its shortcut, or gives a shortcut and asks the action. Wrong-pair variants shift one key to a neighbouring action.
pyqPatterns.approach: Hold the shortcut families: B/I/U formatting trio, Ctrl+= / Ctrl+Shift+= subscript-superscript, Shift+F3 case, Ctrl+Alt+F / Ctrl+Alt+D footnote-endnote, F7 spelling and Shift+F7 thesaurus, Ctrl+Enter page break. When two options look alike, the odd Shift/Alt is usually the truth-teller.

example.q: The keyboard shortcut to change the case of selected text in MS Word is:
example.solution: Shift+F3 — it cycles lowercase, UPPERCASE and Capitalise Each Word. F7 alone runs the spelling check.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Questions on factory defaults: default font and size (Calibri 11 in Word 2007-2021), default view (Print Layout), default alignment (left), default orientation (Portrait), default margins (1 inch).
pyqPatterns.approach: Keep one default card: Calibri 11, Print Layout, left-aligned, Portrait, 1-inch margins, .docx. Beware the version trap — the newest Microsoft 365 builds moved to Aptos 12, so answer Calibri for 2007-2019 stems.

example.q: The default font size in Word 2007 to Word 2019 is:
example.solution: 11 point Calibri — Times New Roman 12 belonged to Word 97-2003.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A scenario: 'send the same letter to 400 customers with each name filled in' or 'print address labels for invitations' — the feature, its components or its tab is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Spot the shape: one fixed document + a list of receivers = mail merge (Mailings tab). Its three parts are the main document, the data source (Excel/Access/Outlook) and the merged output, and the slots in the letter are merge fields like <<Name>>.

example.q: To print 500 admission letters with each student's name and address, the best Word feature is:
example.solution: Mail merge — one main letter joined to a data-source list; Word generates a personalised copy per record.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'On which tab is Track Changes / Page Number / Table of Contents / Margins?' or a matched pair where one feature sits on the wrong tab.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recite the tab map: Home formatting, Insert objects, Design themes, Layout page setup, References TOC-notes-citations, Mailings merge, Review proofing and changes, View views and zoom. The planted traps: Track Changes (Review, not Insert), page numbers (Insert, not Layout), TOC (References, not Insert).

example.q: In MS Word, the Table of Contents option is available on which tab?
example.solution: References — together with footnotes, endnotes and citations.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which one is not a word processor?' or 'which pairing is wrong' with MS Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Access, Outlook in the options.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the family: Word = word processor, Excel = spreadsheet, PowerPoint = presentation, Access = database, Outlook = e-mail and personal organiser. The odd option is usually a famous program pushed into the wrong job (e.g. Excel called a word processor).

example.q: Which of the following is NOT a word processor?
example.solution: MS Excel — it is a spreadsheet program; Word, WordPad and LibreOffice Writer are word processors.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem names a view (Print Layout, Draft, Read Mode, Outline, Web Layout) or a window part (status bar, Quick Access Toolbar, Backstage view) and asks its purpose or default status.
pyqPatterns.approach: Views: Print Layout is the default and print-true; Draft is plain and fast; Read Mode is distraction-free; Outline restructures headings; Web Layout mimics a browser. Window parts: status bar = page number, word count, zoom; File tab = Backstage (New, Open, Print, Options).

example.q: Which window part of MS Word shows 'Page 3 of 12' and the word count?
example.solution: The status bar at the bottom — the title bar only names the file.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Default extension of a Word 2007 document', 'which is the 97-2003 format', or mixed extensions (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx, .docm) where the family rule decides.
pyqPatterns.approach: The X rule: from Office 2007 every default file gained an X — .docx, .xlsx, .pptx (Office Open XML); the X-less forms (.doc, .xls, .ppt) are the 97-2003 formats; an m (.docm, .xlsm, .pptm) always means macro-enabled; t (.dotx) means template.

example.q: A file named report.docm is best described as:
example.solution: A Word 2007+ document that contains macros — m = macro-enabled.

solvedExamples.q: Which shortcut key inserts a hyperlink in MS Word?
solvedExamples.solution: Ctrl+K opens the Insert Hyperlink dialog in all Office apps. Ctrl+H is Find & Replace, Ctrl+N opens a new document, Ctrl+L left-aligns a paragraph.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 'K = linK'. Ctrl+H is the classic trap because H looks like 'hyperlink' but actually means replace.

solvedExamples.q: The default file extension of a document saved in MS Word 2016 is:
solvedExamples.solution: Word 2007 onwards (including 2016) saves documents in Office Open XML format with the .docx extension. .doc is the 97-2003 format, .docm holds macros, .dotx is a template.
solvedExamples.shortcut: X = XML = 2007+. Plain documents take .docx; only macro documents take .docm.

solvedExamples.q:
Statement 1: Mail merge needs a main document and a data source.
Statement 2: An automatic Table of Contents can be generated from manually bolded headings.
solvedExamples.solution: Mail merge indeed combines a main document with a data source (Statement 1 correct). An automatic TOC is built only from Heading styles applied via the Styles gallery - manual bolding carries no heading information, so Statement 2 is wrong.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Remember 'no style, no TOC'. Bold text is formatting, not structure.

solvedExamples.q: Match: (a) Thesaurus (b) Word Count (c) Spelling & Grammar with shortcuts: (i) F7 (ii) Shift+F7 (iii) Ctrl+Shift+G
solvedExamples.solution: F7 runs Spelling & Grammar, Shift+F7 opens the Thesaurus, Ctrl+Shift+G opens the Word Count dialog. Hence a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
solvedExamples.shortcut: F7 = spell; add Shift = thesaurus; add Ctrl as well = word count. The key gets 'heavier' as the tool gets less common.

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following CANNOT be done from the References tab?
solvedExamples.solution: Mail merge lives on the Mailings tab, not References. TOC, footnotes/endnotes, citations and captions are all Reference-tab tools.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Mnemonic: 'Mailings does the Merging'. References only cites and lists.

practice.q: In MS Word, the keyboard shortcut to change the case of selected text (cycling through UPPERCASE, lowercase and Capitalize) is:
practice.solution: Shift+F3 cycles the case of the selection through Sentence case, lowercase, UPPERCASE, Capitalize Each Word and tOGGLE cASE.
practice.shortcut: Three states at your fingertips = F3 (the 3 helps you remember).

practice.q: A page break is inserted in MS Word using:
practice.solution: Ctrl+Enter forces the following text to start on a new page. Ctrl+P prints, Ctrl+B bolds, Alt+Enter has no page-break role in Word.
practice.shortcut: 'Break the page' = press Enter with Ctrl's help: Ctrl+Enter.

practice.q: The default alignment of text in a new MS Word paragraph is:
practice.solution: New paragraphs are left-aligned (ragged right). Justify must be applied deliberately with Ctrl+J.
practice.shortcut: Word starts everything plain: left align, Calibri 11, Print Layout, portrait.

practice.q: Which shortcut key runs the spelling and grammar check in MS Word?
practice.solution: F7 opens Spelling & Grammar. F5 opens Find & Replace's Go To (and starts a PowerPoint show), F9 refreshes fields, F12 is Save As.
practice.shortcut: F7 = spell-check in every Office app.

practice.q: Mail merge in MS Word is used to:
options: Merge two documents into one file
Create personalised copies of a document for many recipients
practice.solution: Mail merge generates letters/labels/envelopes/e-mails where a common main document is personalised from a data source - one template, many recipients.
practice.shortcut: 'Same letter, many names' = mail merge; the trap options play on the word 'merge'.

practice.q: In mail merge, the list of names and addresses (e.g. an Excel sheet) is called the:
practice.solution: The data source supplies the variable values; the main document holds the fixed text; merge fields like «Name» mark where source values appear.
practice.shortcut: Fixed letter = main document; variable list = data source. Fields just point at the source.

practice.q: To generate an automatic Table of Contents, the document's headings must first be formatted with:
practice.solution: The TOC engine reads Heading 1-3 styles (and custom TOC styles). Manually bolded text carries no outline level, so it is ignored.
practice.shortcut: 'No style, no TOC' - the styles gallery, not formatting, feeds the TOC.

practice.q: Track Changes in MS Word is found under which tab?
practice.solution: Track Changes, Comments, Compare, Protect and Word Count are all on the Review tab.
practice.shortcut: Anything about checking/editing text collectively lives in Review.

practice.q: Which shortcut opens the Word Count dialog box?
practice.solution: Ctrl+Shift+G opens Word Count (words, characters with/without spaces, paragraphs, lines). Ctrl+Shift+C copies formatting, Ctrl+Shift+V pastes formatting, Ctrl+Shift+K formats small caps.
practice.shortcut: Word Count = Ctrl+Shift+G ('G for enGlish count' helps some aspirants).

practice.q: The default font of MS Word 2016 documents is:
practice.solution: From Word 2007 to 2021 the default body font is Calibri 11 pt (Times New Roman 12 was the Word 2003 default; Office 365 moved to Aptos 12 in 2023).
practice.shortcut: Eras: 2003 Times New Roman 12 -> 2007-21 Calibri 11 -> 2023+ Aptos 12.

practice.q: Which of the following is a macro-enabled Word document extension?
practice.solution: .docm stores macro-enabled documents; .dotm stores macro-enabled templates. .docx forbids macros, .dotx is a plain template, .rtf is Rich Text Format.
practice.shortcut: The M = Macro: docm/dotm/xlsm/pptm all carry macros.

practice.q: Footnotes inserted with Alt+Ctrl+F appear:
options: At the end of the document
At the bottom of the page where the reference occurs
practice.solution: Footnotes sit at the foot (bottom) of the same page; endnotes (Alt+Ctrl+D) collect at the end of the document or section.
practice.shortcut: Foot = foot of the page; end = end of the document.

practice.q: The keyboard shortcut to increase the indent of a paragraph in MS Word is:
practice.solution: Ctrl+M increases indent, Ctrl+Shift+M decreases it. (Tab indents only at the start of a paragraph/list item; Ctrl+I is italic.)
practice.shortcut: M = More indent; add Shift = less.

practice.q: The superscript formatting shortcut in MS Word is:
practice.solution: Ctrl+Shift+= applies superscript (x squared style); Ctrl+= applies subscript (H2O style). Ctrl+Shift+S opens the Apply Styles box.
practice.shortcut: Shift pushes the number UP: Shift with = gives the raised (super) script.

practice.q: In MS Word, bold, italic and underline buttons are found in the Font group of which tab?
practice.solution: Character formatting lives in the **Font group of the Home tab**. Insert adds objects, View changes views, Layout handles page setup.

practice.q: The option to insert a page number in MS Word is available on the —
practice.solution: Page numbers come from **Insert, Page Number** (usually placed in the header or footer). References holds TOC and footnotes; Review holds proofing tools.

practice.q: Which pair of features is correctly matched with its ribbon tab?
practice.solution: TOC, footnotes, endnotes and citations are all on **References**. Track Changes is Review, margins are Layout, zoom is View/status bar.

practice.q: Which MS Word view shows the document exactly as it will appear when printed?
practice.solution: **Print Layout** (the default view) displays pages, margins and breaks as they will print. Web Layout mimics a web page, Outline works on headings, Draft hides graphics.

practice.q: Reema wants to read a long report without editing tools distracting her. Which view should she use?
practice.solution: **Read Mode** hides the ribbon and shows the text like an e-book. Draft is for fast plain editing, not distraction-free reading.

practice.q: Which view is best suited for rearranging the headings of a long report?
practice.solution: **Outline view** shows only headings and body levels, so whole sections can be dragged up and down to restructure the report.

practice.q: The page number and word count of the open document are shown on the —
practice.solution: The **status bar** at the bottom shows Page x of y, the live word count, language and the zoom slider.

practice.q: Which statement about zoom in MS Word is correct?
options: Zoom changes the font size of the document permanently
Zoom is available only in Draft view
Zoom changes only the on-screen size of the page, not the printed size
Zoom can be changed only from the File tab
practice.solution: Zoom (slider or Ctrl+scroll) is a viewing aid — printing always uses the real font and page sizes.

practice.q: Which key combination opens the Word Count dialog box?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+G** opens the Word Count dialog (also on the Review tab and the status bar). Shift+F7 is the thesaurus; Ctrl+W closes the document.
practice.shortcut: Trap pair: Shift+F7 thesaurus vs Ctrl+Shift+G count.

practice.q: MS Word is a —
practice.solution: Word is the **word processor** of Microsoft Office; Excel is the spreadsheet, PowerPoint the presentation program, Access the database.

practice.q: Which of the following is NOT available in the Backstage view opened by the File tab?
practice.solution: Backstage view handles file-level work: New, Open, Save As, Print, Export, Options. **Formatting commands live on the ribbon**, not in Backstage.
practice.shortcut: File tab = file work, not formatting.

practice.q: Which shortcut key is used to undo the last action in MS Word?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Z = Undo**; Ctrl+Y = Redo, Ctrl+U = underline, Ctrl+A = select all.

practice.q: Why should the Enter key NOT be pressed at the end of every line while typing in Word?
options: Word allows only one Enter per document
Enter turns off word wrap permanently
Word wrap moves text to the next line automatically, so Enter would create broken paragraphs
practice.solution: **Word wrap** breaks lines by itself. Enter should be pressed only to end a paragraph — otherwise editing later becomes messy.

practice.q: The keyboard shortcut for Italics in MS Word is —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+I = Italic**; Ctrl+K inserts a hyperlink, Ctrl+J justifies, Ctrl+P prints.

practice.q: Which shortcut places selected text as a subscript?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+= = subscript** (H2O); the Shift version, Ctrl+Shift+=, gives superscript (x squared style).

practice.q: Pressing Shift+F3 with a word selected in MS Word —
options: Cycles the case between lowercase, UPPERCASE and Capitalise Each Word
practice.solution: **Shift+F3 is the Change Case shortcut** — tap it repeatedly to cycle. Thesaurus is Shift+F7.

practice.q: Which shortcut pair is correctly matched?
practice.solution: Ctrl+Shift+> grows the font size and Ctrl+< shrinks it. Ctrl+D opens the Font dialog, not underline (Ctrl+U).

practice.q: Which shortcut key centres the selected paragraph in MS Word?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+E = centre** (E for cEntrE). Ctrl+J justifies, Ctrl+M indents, Ctrl+C copies.

practice.q: In MS Word, Ctrl+J is used to —
options: Justify the paragraph so both edges are aligned
practice.solution: **Ctrl+J = Justify** — the text is stretched so the left AND right margins are straight, as in newspapers.

practice.q: What is the default text alignment of a new MS Word document?
practice.solution: A new document is **left-aligned**: the right edge stays ragged unless you change it.

practice.q: Which shortcut applies single line spacing in MS Word?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+1 = single**, Ctrl+5 = 1.5 lines, Ctrl+2 = double line spacing.

practice.q: To start a new page immediately from the current cursor position, press —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Enter inserts a page break**. Shift+Enter is only a soft line break; Ctrl+P prints.

practice.q: A student typed 1.5 at the start of a line and the paragraph spacing changed to 1.5 lines. Which key caused it?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+5 sets 1.5 line spacing** — a classic accidental shortcut. Ctrl+2 is double, Ctrl+1 single.

practice.q: The default orientation of an MS Word page is —
practice.solution: New pages are **Portrait** (taller than wide). Landscape is chosen manually on the Layout tab.

practice.q: In the default (Normal) margin setting, the blank space around an MS Word page is —
practice.solution: Normal margins are **1 inch (2.54 cm) on top, bottom, left and right**.

practice.q: A wide marksheet table keeps getting cut at the right edge. Which change helps most?
options: Change the page orientation to Landscape
practice.solution: **Landscape** widens the page (Layout tab, Orientation) so wide tables fit. Zoom only changes the screen view.

practice.q: The default font of documents created in Word 2007 to Word 2019 is —
practice.solution: Office 2007 onwards used **Calibri 11 pt**. Times New Roman 12 was the pre-2007 default; Aptos 12 ships only in the newest Microsoft 365 builds.

practice.q: Font size in MS Word is measured in —
practice.solution: Font size uses **points** (72 points = 1 inch of character height). Page size uses inches or centimetres.

practice.q: Mail merge in MS Word is used to —
options: Merge two Word files into one
Join two tables side by side
Create many personalised documents from one template and a data list
practice.solution: **Mail merge** produces one finished copy per record — same letter body, different names and addresses.

practice.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of mail merge?
practice.solution: The three components are the **main document, the data source and the merged output**. Headers/footers are page furniture, unrelated to merging.

practice.q: In mail merge, the placeholder <<City>> inserted in the main document is called a —
practice.solution: **Merge fields** (shown inside double angle brackets) mark where each data-source value will be filled in.

practice.q: Arrange the mail-merge steps in order: 1. Preview results 2. Write the main document 3. Attach the data source 4. Insert merge fields
practice.solution: Write the letter, attach the data source, insert merge fields, preview, then finish and merge.

practice.q: A footnote in MS Word appears at the —
practice.solution: **Footnotes print at the foot (bottom) of the page**; endnotes are collected at the end of the document or section.

practice.q: The shortcut to insert an endnote in MS Word is —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Alt+D = endnote** (D for enD); Ctrl+Alt+F = footnote (F is right under your fingers for 'foot').

practice.q: An automatic Table of Contents in Word can be generated only if the headings use —
practice.solution: TOC reads the **style names** (Heading 1, Heading 2...), not the visual look — manually bolded lines are invisible to it.

practice.q: After editing a report, its Table of Contents shows wrong page numbers. The fastest fix is —
options: Update the field (right-click, Update Field or F9)
practice.solution: The TOC is a **field** — one update (F9) re-reads the headings and refreshes every page number.

practice.q: Which key runs the spelling and grammar check in MS Word?
practice.solution: **F7 = Spelling & Grammar**. F5 starts a slideshow in PowerPoint but in Word it opens Go To.

practice.q: Which feature marks every insertion and deletion made by co-authors?
practice.solution: **Track Changes** (Review tab, Ctrl+Shift+E) records each edit so reviewers can accept or reject it later.

practice.q: To attach a virtual sticky note to a selected sentence for a reviewer, use —
practice.solution: **Comments** are margin notes attached to text (Review tab, Ctrl+Alt+M). They print separately and can be resolved or deleted.

practice.q: Before enabling macros in a document, Word shows a warning mainly because —
practice.solution: A macro is runnable code, so a **macro virus** can hide inside a .docm file and run when opened — hence the warning bar.

practice.q: Which file extension is used for a macro-enabled Word document?
practice.solution: **m = macro**: .docm for documents, .dotm for macro templates. Plain .docx cannot store macros.

practice.q: The default extension of a Word 2007 or later document is —
practice.solution: **.docx** is the Office Open XML default from Word 2007 onwards; .doc is the 97-2003 file.

practice.q: In the extension .docx, the letter X stands for —
practice.solution: The X marks the **Office Open XML** format introduced with Office 2007 — the same X appears in .xlsx and .pptx.

practice.q: A document saved in Word 97-2003 format carries which extension?
practice.solution: The old binary format is **.doc**; X-less extensions are always the pre-2007 formats.

practice.q: Word 2003 cannot open a .docx file directly. What did Microsoft provide for this?
practice.solution: The free **Compatibility Pack** let old Word versions open and save the new XML formats.
practice.shortcut: Old Word + pack = opens new files.

practice.q: Which extension belongs to a Word template?
practice.solution: Templates carry **t**: .dotx (plain) and .dotm (with macros). Opening one creates a fresh untitled copy.

practice.q: What happens when a .dotx template file is opened?
options: A new untitled document based on the template opens
The template itself opens for editing
practice.solution: Templates protect their design: Word gives you a **fresh copy** (Document1, Document2...) built on the template.

practice.q: Which format should be used to e-mail a document that must print identically everywhere?
practice.solution: **PDF** freezes fonts, layout and pictures on every device and printer.

practice.q: Which extension stores plain text with NO formatting at all?
practice.solution: **.txt** keeps only characters — no bold, fonts, colours or images. .rtf keeps simple formatting, .odt and .docx keep full formatting.

practice.q: Match the column: 1. .rtf 2. .odt 3. .pdf — a. OpenDocument text b. fixed print layout c. Rich Text Format
practice.solution: .rtf = Rich Text Format, .odt = OpenDocument Text (free office suites), .pdf = fixed print layout.
practice.shortcut: R = Rich, O = Open, P = Print.

practice.q: Which file CANNOT be created by MS Word's own Save As list?
practice.solution: Word saves documents (.docx, .doc, .dotx, .docm), PDF, XPS, web page, .rtf and .odt — but **.pptx belongs to PowerPoint**, a different program.
